content: 1. In the South-East Asia Region, humans are recognized as the sole reservoir for Leishmania donovani, the causative agent of kala-azar. 2. The sandfly species Phlebotomus argentipes is the only known vector responsible for the transmission of L. donovani in this region. 3. The geographical distribution of kala-azar is restricted to specific, well-defined areas in a few countries within the South-East Asia Region. 4. Effective diagnostic tools, such as the rK39-based rapid diagnostic test (RDT), and safe, efficacious treatment options are available for managing kala-azar. 5. High-level political commitment has been demonstrated through the signing of a memorandum of understanding by health ministers of endemic countries, aimed at the regional elimination of kala-azar. 6. Efforts by Member States, guided by the Regional Technical Advisory Group (RTAG) and the Regional Strategic Framework, and supported by donors and research partners, have progressively enhanced the capacity for passive and active case detection, diagnosis, case management, vector surveillance, and control measures to achieve kala-azar elimination. 7. These advancements were made possible through: Strong political commitment and allocation of dedicated resources by Member States. Partnerships for research and innovation, enabling rapid translation of findings into effective strategies, policies, and practices. Timely donor support to improve access to essential drugs, diagnostics, and public health interventions. 8. Between 2007 and 2021, significant progress was achieved, with 99% of implementation units (IUs) in Bangladesh, India, and Nepal meeting the elimination target of less than one kala-azar case per 10,000 population. Only 1% of IUs remained above the elimination threshold. 9. Bangladesh has sustained the elimination target in all IUs since 2017, with a substantial decline in new kala-azar cases reported across the region. 10. Despite these achievements, several gaps and emerging challenges remain in accelerating and sustaining kala-azar elimination. 11. Current tools are suboptimal for preventing infection and interrupting parasite transmission. The rK39 RDT, while effective, cannot distinguish between active and past infections and remains positive for years. 12. Post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis (PKDL) cases require prolonged treatment, often leading to poor treatment adherence. The safety of long-duration treatments has not been adequately studied. 13. Diagnosis and treatment of kala-azar-HIV co-infections require specialized capacity at tertiary healthcare facilities, and risk factors for relapse and appropriate treatment options remain under debate. 14. Integrated vector management (IVM), including indoor residual spraying (IRS), is a key strategy for vector control. However, IRS is resource-intensive and may not be sustainable in the long term, with limited alternative vector control tools available. 15. Kala-azar outbreaks continue to be reported from endemic, formerly endemic, and non-endemic areas, potentially due to waning herd immunity as case numbers decline. 16. The COVID-19 pandemic has disrupted neglected tropical disease (NTD) interventions, including active case detection, IRS activities, and community awareness campaigns, necessitating renewed investment in surveillance, case management, and vector control strategies. 17. Sustained vigilance is critical to prevent resurgence and maintain the gains achieved in kala-azar elimination efforts. 18. Continued research and development (R&D) are essential to optimize diagnostic tools, develop safe and effective oral therapies, and integrate these advancements into primary healthcare systems. 19. Strengthening surveillance systems, including geospatial mapping, syndromic surveillance, and population-based serosurveillance, is vital for monitoring trends and sustaining elimination efforts. 20. Collaboration with private healthcare providers and dermatologists is crucial to ensure comprehensive case detection and management, particularly for PKDL and kala-azar-HIV co-infections. 21. Mechanisms to track and follow up on migration of cases within and between countries are necessary, especially in the post-validation phase, to address the spread of cases to new areas. 22. National notification systems for kala-azar and PKDL should be reinforced, and indicators established to monitor surveillance performance and ensure timely reporting and referral of suspected cases. 23. Integration of kala-azar elimination strategies with other public health programs will contribute to strengthening overall health system capacity and achieving universal health coverage. 24. Sustained investment in R&D and operational research is required to address gaps in treatment guidelines, improve case management, and monitor the safety and effectiveness of current and new treatments.
